summary:
Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021. The lower house of Parliament voted 43-1 in June 2019 to repeal Penal Code Sections 213 and 214, the 'unnatural sex' provisions carrying one month to one year of imprisonment, which had gone unenforced for at least 15 years. The upper house reinserted the ban, and a December 2020 joint sitting resolved that homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex. The Penal Code Amendment Act entered into force on 17 February 2021, and no reversal has followed.

The repeal created no protective framework. Bhutan has no stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit protections on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and sex characteristics. Discrimination and stigma persist, with health-care access singled out as a domain where trans and LGBTIQ people are turned away or poorly served.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable: administrative gender-marker changes are suspended for lack of standardised guidelines. Where markers can be changed at all, the process requires a medical note plus a supporting letter from a civil society organisation. Trans people are over four times more likely to experience assault than the general population. A 49-year-old trans woman interviewed by Bhutan Broadcasting Service in November 2024 reported that police dismiss her cases because her identity card reads male, telling her 'both parties are men'; families pressure victims to accept violence as fate, and help routed through the LGBTQIA+ committee is slow. The result is practical impunity for anti-trans violence despite formal decriminalisation.

Public trans visibility exists but remains exceptional. One of only two publicly living trans women, Dechen, fought at age 16 to wear the female school uniform kira, a first in Bhutanese society. LGBTIQ organisations may register, though activists describe the process as lengthy and burdensome.

Bhutan provides no legal recognition of same-sex relationships, and partners of trans and other LGBTQ people cannot be recognised in any legal proceeding. A marriage bill using gender-neutral pronouns was discussed during the 2018 summer parliamentary session but deferred due to the 2018 parliamentary election.

Some institutional protections exist. The Bhutan Medical and Health Council's Code of Professional Fidelity, issued in 2021, protects sexual orientation. The 2020 Standard Operating Procedure for Gender Based Violence Prevention and Response requires healthcare providers to deliver care sensitive to sexual orientation and gender identity, and requires case managers to provide tailored care for people of diverse orientations and identities. The National Strategic Framework on Comprehensive Sexuality Education (2021) covers LGBTI issues.

State engagement has increased. The 2024 Free & Equal campaign trained the Royal Court of Justice, Attorney General's Office and Cabinet Secretariat, and secured the first-ever direct dialogue between Bhutan's LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians; two consultation workshops convened community members with UN and National Commission for Women and Children representatives.
tangentialFactors:
Social invisibility compounds legal risk. Reporting from 2015 described near-total social invisibility for LGBT Bhutanese, with no shared language for gay or trans identities and lesbianism under-recognised; one public figure described growing up gay in Bhutan as 'a very alienating experience'. The LGBT Bhutan Facebook page, founded in 2013, produced the country's first public affirmation of a gay population.

Education remains a hostile environment: Rainbow Bhutan's director states most LGBTQ youths drop out of school, and of the 316 people registered as LGBTQ in 2019, 10 were below age 19.
localsOnly:
Registration of LGBTIQ organisations is possible but activists call the process lengthy and burdensome. Gender-marker changes on legal identification documents require a medical note plus a supporting letter from a civil society organisation, though broader administrative changes are suspended pending standardised guidelines.

Institutional capacity-building is underway: the 2024 Free & Equal campaign trained the Royal Court of Justice, Attorney General's Office and Cabinet Secretariat, and produced the first direct dialogue between the LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians. Two consultation workshops brought community members together with UN and National Commission for Women and Children representatives.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the deferred 2018 gender-neutral marriage bill under the current Parliament is unresolved in these sources; Rainbow Bhutan's director said the community expected the conversation to be revived, but no subsequent legislative action is sourced here.

Whether the suspended administrative gender-marker process has since been replaced by standardised guidelines is not sourced. The claim that trans people are over four times more likely to experience assault comes from a single broadcast report and the underlying study is not cited.
